endorsements.quote: Limited high-stakes rollout is reserved for stations where behavioral anchors are clear and AI‑extracted evidence is demonstrably reliable under human supervision.
Assessment assistants prescore specific behaviors or extract time-stamped evidence mapped to rubric items so that raters can verify, edit, or reject suggestions.
These rater actions are logged alongside time-stamped evidence links and model or prompt versions and summarized in dashboards tracking error modes, drift signals, and subgroup differences.
Logs should record model versions, prompts, rater decisions, and time-stamped evidence to enable drift detection and recalibration.
Cohort dashboards track blueprint coverage, rater effects, and subgroup performance differences to support continuous improvement and equity monitoring.

Institutions should prefer tools that publish model cards and data sheets, expose application programming interfaces for log capture, support role-based access, and report subgroup performance [ 22 , 23 ].
When using third-party models, they require disclosures consistent with model cards and data sheets and insist on contractual guarantees for security and incident response [ 22 - 24 ].
Safety checklists and red teaming apply to AI-SP prompts and assessment assistant outputs before deployment and after significant model updates.

When subgroup gaps are detected, corrective actions target persona prompts, rubric anchors, or instructional supports and are followed by reevaluation, consistent with fairness-by-design practices [ 22 , 25 ].

In high-stakes settings, optimization should preferentially occur through governance-layer updates (persona cards, prompt sets, rubric anchors, and extraction rules) because they are auditable and reversible; model retraining or fine-tuning is treated as a higher-risk intervention requiring explicit approval, revalidation, and a rollback plan.
Equity indicators track subgroup differences in scores, rater edits to AI suggestions, and the accessibility of feedback.

Phase 3 (limited high‑stakes use) includes restricting deployment to stations with clear behavioral anchors, requiring a real‑time kill switch and escalation route, implementing an appeal pathway supported by traceable logs, and scaling only if predefined reliability, equity, and workload gates are met.
Mock OSCEs introduce AI‑assisted stations and compare conditions with and without AI support to quantify benefits and harms in context.
Human assessors have final authority, and every AI suggestion comes with a rationale linked to auditable evidence, consistent with explainability by design [ 21 ].
Transparency with students and faculty about what AI is used for, what purpose it serves, and what evidence is retained is essential.
Transparency artifacts—model cards and data sheets—document intended use, data sources, and limitations so that faculty can supervise with eyes open [ 22 , 23 ].

unlisted_practices: Default to data minimization and deidentification, collecting only information needed for assessment, feedback, and improvement, with role-based access and policy-set log retention.
Use federated analytics with only aggregate sharing when cross-border data transfer constraints are substantial.
Establish a shared deidentified registry with harmonized rubric vocabularies to benchmark reliability, validity, equity, and workload across sites.
Require faculty review and sign-off before any AI-generated case enters mock or high-stakes use.
Constrain AI-standardized-patient responses using persona cards with defined response boundaries and approved domains.
Consider fine-tuning only where there is a clear legal basis and robust controls including dataset provenance documentation, data minimization, and predeployment safety, bias, and leakage testing.

screen.reason: This is a viewpoint/framework paper presenting recommendations and governance approaches for AI-augmented OSCEs in nursing education, rather than presenting original empirical data.
